title: Antibiotic-resistant infections in primary care are symptomatic for longer and increase workload: outcomes for patients with E. coli UTIs.
authors: Butler CC, Hillier S, Roberts Z, Dunstan F, Howard A, Palmer S
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is considered to be one of the major threats to public health. However, the practical implications for patients and workload in primary care are largely unknown. To determine outcomes for patients managed in primary care with an antibiotic resistant compared to an antibiotic sensitive Escherichia coli (E. coli) urinary tract infection (UTI). Nested case control study with prospective measurement of outcomes. Ten general practices in South Wales. Patients consulting with symptoms suggestive of UTI identified through systematic sampling, and with a laboratory proven E. coli infection, were followed up by interview 1 month after their consultations and by searching of their medical records. Nine hundred and thirty-two patients were interviewed and had their medical records reviewed. The risk of patients reporting 'feeling poorly', 'frequency or pain on urinating' and being 'out of action' for more than 5 days after consulting was significantly increased for patients with resistant compared to sensitive infections. After adjusting for risk factors, there was an increased risk of 'frequency or pain on urinating' and 'being out of action' for those infected with a resistant E. coli. The median number of maximum reported days with at least one symptom was 12 days for patients with E. coli infections resistant to trimethoprim, 7 days for infections resistant to ampicillin, 7 days for infections resistant to any antibiotic, and 5 days for infections sensitive to all tested antibiotics. Even if treated with an appropriate antibiotic, infections caused by a resistant strain were symptomatic for longer. For those infected with an organism resistant to at least one antibiotic, the odds ratio (OR) for re-visiting their GP within the next 30 days for the UTI was 1.47 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.10 to 1.95). The OR was 1.49 (95% CI = 1.11 to 2.00) for ampicillin resistance and 2.48 (95% CI = 1.70 to 3.59) for trimethoprim resistance. Resistant E. coli UTIs are symptomatic for longer and cause increased work load in general practice.

(4) Exposure is not prophylactic antibiotic use directed at preventing rUTI recurrences. (5) Reports clinically relevant outcomes and some resistance information (resistant vs sensitive E. coli). title: Intensive care unit-acquired urinary tract infections in patients admitted with sepsis: etiology, risk factors, and patterns of antimicrobial resistance.
authors: Mojtahedzadeh M, Panahi Y, Fazeli MR, Najafi A, Pazouki M, Navehsi BM, Bazzaz A, Naghizadeh MM, Beiraghdar F
abstract: The objective of the present study was to evaluate the etiology, risk factors, and patterns of antimicrobial resistance of intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired urinary tract infections (UTIs) in patients admitted with sepsis. In this observational study, 100 septic patients hospitalized in a general ICU were selected. Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were obtained by chart review. Antibiotic resistance/susceptibility was determined using the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) technique. A UTI was present in 28 (28%) patients; the male to female ratio was 19:9 and the mean age of the patients was 58.71+/-19.45 years. From the total of 28 isolates, 27 were resistant to ciprofloxacin, 23 to amikacin, 27 to meropenem, 28 to cefepime, 26 to ceftazidime, and 27 to ceftriaxone. On the basis of our results, the rate of multidrug-resistant UTIs may be very high in some ICUs in patients admitted with sepsis. This antimicrobial susceptibility/resistance should be determined, and a special antimicrobial treatment protocol should be planned based on the results for each ICU. The use of antibiotics for treating UTIs should be guided only through this protocol because of the different spectra of pathogens and susceptibility patterns in each ICU.

abstract: We investigated the frequency and characteristics of infectious purulent and non-infectious complications in living related renal transplant recipients in early postoperative period. The prevention and treatment schemes, antimicrobial drugs dosing regimen were developed. It leads to decrease the infectious complications rate.

title: The impact of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia prophylaxis on the occurrence of asymptomatic bacteriuria and urinary tract infections among renal allograft recipients: a retrospective before-after study.
authors: Singh R, Bemelman FJ, Hodiamont CJ, Idu MM, Ten Berge IJ, Geerlings SE
abstract: The international guidelines recommend the administration of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) as Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis for six months after transplantation. The aim of this study is to evaluate the influence of TMP-SMX prophylaxis on the occurrence of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) and urinary tract infections (UTIs) as cystitis and allograft pyelonephritis (AGPN) and its impact on the antimicrobial resistance pattern of causative microorganisms. We have conducted a retrospective before-after study in adult renal allograft recipients with one year follow-up after transplantation. We compared the ("after") group that received TMP-SMX as PJP prophylaxis to the ("before") group that did not receive it. In total, 343 renal allograft recipients were analysed, of whom 212 (61.8 %) received TMP-SMX as PJP prophylaxis. In this study, 63 (18.4 %) did only develop ASB without UTI, 26 (7.6 %) developed cystitis and 43 (12.5 %) developed AGPN. The remaining 211 (61.5 %) renal allograft recipients did not develop any bacteriuria at all. Multivariable Cox proportional regression analysis indicated that TMP-SMX as PJP prophylaxis was not associated with reduced prevalence of ASB (Hazard ratio (HR) = 1.52, 95 % CI = 0.79-2.94, p = 0.213), nor with reduced incidence of cystitis (HR = 2.21, 95 % CI = 0.76-6.39, p = 0.144), nor AGPN (HR = 1.12, 95 % CI = 0.57-2.21, p = 0.751). Among the group receiving TMP-SMX as PJP prophylaxis there was a trend was observed in increase of both amoxicillin (86 % versus 70 %) and TMP-SMX (89 % versus 48 %) resistance which already appeared within the first 30 days after TMP-SMX exposure. Among renal allograft recipients, administration of TMP-SMX as PJP prophylaxis does not prevent ASB nor UTI, however it is associated with tendency towards increased amoxicillin and TMP-SMX resistance.

Population/setting: retrospective before-after study in clinical transplant recipients (real-world healthcare context). Intervention: TMP-SMX prophylaxis exposure is clearly evaluated. Outcome: reports antimicrobial resistance pattern of causative microorganisms (amoxicillin and TMP-SMX resistance) with timing (within 30 days) and resistance percentages. Study design: original retrospective before-after cohort (not a systematic review/meta-analysis).

title: General practitioners' perspectives on diagnosis and treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections: A qualitative study in the Northern Dutch-German cross-border region.
authors: Bedri A, Mulderij-Jansen V, Aits I, Berends M, Freitag MH, van der Worp H, Glasner C, Blanker MH
abstract: In the Netherlands and Germany, most antibiotics are prescribed in primary care, with urinary tract infections (UTIs) being the most common reason. The resistance rates of pathogens causing UTIs are rising in Europe. Differences in clinical practice guidelines may play a role and influence the prevalence of antibiotic resistance and treatment options. Therefore, we aim to explore the reality of general practices, including the diagnosis and management of uncomplicated UTIs in the Northern Dutch-German cross-border region. From January 2023 to April 2024, a qualitative study was performed using semi-structured interviews with German and Dutch general practitioners (GPs). The number of interviews was determined when data saturation was reached. The interviews were recorded, transcribed, translated and anonymised. MAXQDA (Version 24.1.0.) was utilised to code the interviews. The analysis was done using structured qualitative content analysis. We recruited 13 GPs in Germany and 10 GPs in the Netherlands. Four main themes were identified: diagnosis, treatment options, decision making and guidelines. Dutch GPs delegated most diagnosis and treatment tasks to practice assistants, which is facilitated by the more stringent use of guidelines. More variety was seen in the types of antibiotics and herbal remedies used by German GPs. This study provides valuable insights into GPs' decision making regarding the diagnosis and treatment of UTI. Increasing awareness of UTI diagnosis and treatment can help GPs assess their own practices and think more critically of their antibiotic use. Further research is needed to explore the effects on antibiotic resistance in the cross-border region.

While not specifically a prophylactic antibiotic regimen in rUTI patients, it is clearly within the UTI treatment domain and addresses antibiotic use; the abstract mentions rising resistance and guideline-driven variability, so resistance outcomes are at least plausibly relevant (though not measured). Design appears to be an original qualitative study, not a review/meta-analysis.

title: Antibiotic resistance pattern among common bacterial uropathogens with a special reference to ciprofloxacin resistant Escherichia coli.
authors: Mandal J, Acharya NS, Buddhapriya D, Parija SC
abstract: The resistance of bacteria causing urinary tract infection (UTI) to commonly prescribed antibiotics is increasing both in developing as well as in developed countries. Resistance has emerged even to more potent antimicrobial agents. The present study was undertaken to report the current antibiotic resistance pattern among common bacterial uropathogens isolated in a tertiary care hospital in south India, with a special reference to ciprofloxacin. A total of 19,050 consecutive urine samples were cultured and pathogens isolated were identified by standard methods. Antibiotic susceptibility was done by Kirby Bauer disk diffusion method. The clinical and demographic profile of the patients was noted. Of the 19,050 samples, 62 per cent were sterile, 26.01 per cent showed significant growth, 2.3 per cent showed insignificant growth and 9.6 per cent were found contaminated. Significant association (P<0.001) of prior use of antibiotics in males, UTI in adults, gynaecological surgery in females, obstructive uropathy in males and complicated UTI in females with the occurrence of UTI with ciprofloxacin resistant Escherichia coli was noted. Significant association was noted in females with prior antibiotics, with prior urological surgery and in males with prior complicated UTI. There was no significant association with diabetes mellitus with the occurrence of UTI with ciprofloxacin resistant E. coli. Fluoroquinolone resistance was found to increase with age. INTERPRETATIONS & CONCLUSIONS: Ciprofloxacin resistance has emerged due to its frequent use. This resistance was seen more in the in-patients, elderly males and females. Also the resistance to other antibiotics was also high. Increasing antibiotic resistance trends indicate that it is imperative to rationalize the use of antimicrobials in the community and also use these conservatively.
reviewer_1_rationale: Tertiary-care hospital study of patients with UTIs; assesses antibiotic susceptibility/resistance patterns of uropathogens with attention to ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli and associations with prior antibiotic use. Outcomes include resistance (phenotypes/susceptibility) and relevant clinical factors. Appears to be an original observational resistance survey rather than a systematic review.

Resistance outcomes are directly measured: antibiotic susceptibility by Kirby–Bauer disk diffusion with emphasis on ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli (and other uropathogens). Prior antibiotic use is analyzed for association with ciprofloxacin-resistant E. coli occurrence. Original observational study (large consecutive urine culture dataset), not a review.

title: An Ambulatory Antimicrobial Stewardship Initiative to Improve Diagnosis and Treatment of Urinary Tract Infections in Children.
authors: Walters EM, D'Auria J, Jackson C, Walsh-Kelly C, Park D, Willis ZI
journal: Jt Comm J Qual Patient Saf
abstract: Antibiotic stewardship efforts should standardize treatment of common infections when possible. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common in children and require appropriate diagnostic methods and treatment. A pediatric emergency department (ED) identified an opportunity to improve care by standardizing uncomplicated UTI diagnostic testing and treatment according to local bacterial resistance patterns from January 2017 to December 2018. Using the Model for Improvement, researchers undertook a quality improvement (QI) initiative to standardize the diagnosis and treatment of uncomplicated UTI in children ages 3 months to 12 years in a pediatric ED. Multiple Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles were used, engaging both nurses and physicians, to implement an evidence-based clinical algorithm. Primary aims were to achieve 100% of targeted patients with suspected UTI having appropriately ordered and collected specimens and to increase the frequency of targeted patients receiving algorithm-recommended antibiotics at discharge to 80%. Balancing measures included ED length of stay and revisits to the ED related to UTI. During this initiative, 458 children were assessed for UTI, of whom 75 received a UTI diagnosis. Guideline-concordant urine collection procedure improved from 54.7% to 96.2%. After project initiation, 100% of all antibiotic prescriptions for UTI were guideline-concordant. These changes have been sustained for 19 months since the initiative began. There was no change in UTI-related ED revisits or ED length of stay. This QI initiative achieved standardization of specimen collection and treatment for pediatric UTI in the ED setting, and no adverse outcomes were observed at the institution.

(3) Intervention is an antimicrobial stewardship/QI initiative standardizing UTI diagnosis and treatment with antibiotic recommendations. (4) Focus is on UTI treatment algorithms aligned with local bacterial resistance patterns, indicating antibiotics directed at the UTI process. Given the broad resistance-relevant stewardship context, still plausible. (6) Not a systematic review/meta-analysis; described as an original quality improvement initiative.

title: The role of host factors and bacterial virulence genes in the development of pyelonephritis caused by Escherichia coli in renal transplant recipients.
authors: Siliano PR, Rocha LA, Medina-Pestana JO, Heilberg IP
abstract: The aim of this study was to determine the role of host factors and bacterial virulence genes in the development of pyelonephritis caused by Escherichia coli in renal transplant (Tx) recipients. A total of 328 E. coli isolates from cases of cystitis (Cys; n=239) or pyelonephritis (PN; n=89), with 169 from renal Tx recipients, were subjected to molecular analyses to identify P-fimbria subunits (PapC, PapG II, and PapGIII), G- and M-fimbriae, and aerobactin. The presence of antibiotic resistance was also determined. Parameters such as gender, age, immunosuppression regimens, causes of ESRD, kidney donor, intraoperative anastomosis, use of double J stent, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ) prophylaxis, and time after Tx were evaluated. A multivariate analysis showed a significant association between PN and renal Tx. In renal Tx recipients, the risk of occurrence of PN was significantly higher among males and for those no longer receiving TMP/SMZ prophylaxis. E. coli strains isolated from PN presented a lower prevalence of papGIII and lower rates of resistance to pipemidic acid. Although papGII was more prevalent in PN than in Cys, it was not independently associated with PN. These findings suggested that renal Tx increases the risk for PN, and the male sex represented a host factor independently associated with risk, whereas the prophylaxis with TMP/SMZ was protective. The lack of papGIII and low resistance to first-generation quinolones were bacterial-independent risk factors for PN in Tx.
reviewer_1_rationale: Population includes renal transplant recipients with recurrent/past cystitis and pyelonephritis episodes (human clinical context). The study assesses TMP/SMZ prophylaxis exposure (antibiotic prophylaxis) and compares outcomes in cystitis vs pyelonephritis, with resistance phenotypes measured in E. coli isolates. Outcomes include clinically relevant infection outcome (pyelonephritis) and antibiotic resistance rates. It is an original observational molecular/resistance study (not a systematic review).

Outcome is pyelonephritis occurrence (within O domain via resistance reporting and prophylaxis association with PN risk). Not a review/meta-analysis.

title: Changing pattern of antimicrobial susceptibility of organisms causing community acquired urinary tract infections.
authors: Farooqi BJ, Shareeq F, Rizvi QK, Qureshi HS, Ashfaq MK
abstract: To assess common organisms causing Urinary Treat Infection (UTI) in this community and to see antimicrobial susceptibility pattern of these isolates. Prospective study on urine samples. Tertiary care hospital in Karachi. Over a period of 8 years (1990-97) 9,892 urine samples grew significant bacteriuria for various organisms. All Gram negative rods and entercocci was identified by using API 20E and API 32 strips respectively. Staphylococci were identified by catalase, coagulase and D'Nase tests. Antimicrobial sensitivity testing of all isolates was performed on Diagnostic Sensitivity Test plates by Kerby Bauer method. The discs used were ampicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, aztreonam, ofloxacin, carbenicillin, amikacin, gentamicin, penicillin, clindamycin, methicillin, vancomycin, ceftazidime, cefuroxime, Nalidixic acid, pipemedic acid and Nitrofurantoin. Our results indicate that E. coli and Klebsiella aerogenes are the most common organisms causing UTI in this community. Other organisms involved are Pseudomonas aeroginosa, Enterobacter species, Enterococcus, Proteus mirabillus, Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus saprophyticus. Organisms resistant to various antimicrobial agents such as gentamicin, Amikacin, Ofloxacin, Cefotaxime and Ceftazidime are increasing. In conclusion, E. coli and Klebsiella aerogenes are the most common organisms causing UTI in this community. Pattern of antibiotic susceptibility to first line antibiotics is changing. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing of all isolates is crucial for the treatment of UTI.
reviewer_1_rationale: The study is in a human clinical setting (tertiary care hospital) and assesses organisms from urine samples with UTI, reporting antimicrobial susceptibility/resistance trends. However, it does not involve women with recurrent UTIs, and it does not evaluate prophylactic antibiotic exposure/regimens. Outcomes fall within resistance/susceptibility domains, and it appears to be an original prospective resistance surveillance study (not a systematic review).
reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Targets human urinary tract infection isolates, relevant to women with recurrent UTIs (population likely matches, though not explicitly women). 2) Conducted in a tertiary care hospital setting with community-acquired UTI samples. 3) Assesses antibiotic susceptibility (a relevant resistance exposure domain) and trends over time. 4) Antibiotics tested are directed at UTI pathogens (not an unrelated intervention). 5) Reports antimicrobial resistance trends/susceptibility patterns among uropathogens (within outcome domain, though no prophylaxis effect). 6) Described as a prospective original study over 8 years, not a systematic review.

title: Bacterial resistance in urinary tract infections in patients with diabetes matched with patients without diabetes.
authors: Malmartel A, Ghasarossian C
abstract: With bacterial resistances having increased, patients with diabetes who are at higher risk of urinary tract infection (UTI) need to be studied. The study aim was to compare bacterial resistances to ofloxacin, cefixim, co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin in UTI between patients with and without diabetes. A cross-sectional study was conducted in ambulatory laboratories, including patients over 18 coming for urinalyses. Patients with diabetes were matched with two patients without diabetes based on risk factors for UTI using a propensity score. Among 1119 patients with UTI, 124 patients with diabetes were matched with 246 patients without diabetes. In patients with diabetes, the bacteria identified were: Escherichia coli (71%), Klebsiella (6%), Staphylococcus (5%), Enterococcus (4%), Proteus (2%) and Pseudomonas (1%); these findings were similar to those found in patients without diabetes. Resistances to ofloxacin and cefixim regardless of the bacteria were increased in patients with diabetes after matching on age, sex and history of UTI (respectively: OR=2.09; p=0.04 and OR=3.67; p=0.05). Regarding E. coli resistance, there was no difference whatever the antibiotic. The increased ofloxacin and cefixim resistance in patients with diabetes should be considered when prescribing probabilistic antibiotics, and could lead to changes in first-line treatments in UTI.

title: Extended antimicrobial use in patients undergoing percutaneous nephrolithotomy and associated antibiotic related complications.
authors: Viers BR, Cockerill PA, Mehta RA, Bergstralh EJ, Krambeck AE
abstract: Despite global concern about antibiotic related complications the duration of antibiotic therapy at percutaneous nephrolithotomy varies based on individual physician practice. We evaluated perioperative antibiotic related complications in patients who received extended antimicrobial therapy at percutaneous nephrolithotomy. We reviewed the records of 227 consecutive patients treated with percutaneous nephrolithotomy from 2009 to 2013. Patients with positive urine or stone cultures received extended antimicrobial treatment. All others received 7 days of empirical therapy preoperatively and postoperatively. Adverse antibiotic related events were recorded for up to 3 months. The median duration of antibiotic therapy was 14 days (IQR 14-34). Perioperatively 143 (63%), 67 (30%), 75 (33%) and 41 patients (18%) received nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones and other antibiotics, respectively. Antibiotic related complications developed in 23 patients (10%) at a median of 12 days (IQR 8-19). Common complications included rash in 7 cases (3%), gastrointestinal upset in 6 (3%) and Clostridium difficile colitis in 1 (0.4%). Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was associated with an increased likelihood of an adverse event (p = 0.04) but patient age, gender, and therapy type (therapeutic vs prophylactic) and duration were not. Finally, antibiotic and multidrug resistance developed in 4 (36%) and 3 patients (27%), respectively, who experienced a urinary tract infection. We report a low rate of adverse antibiotic related events in patients treated with percutaneous nephrolithotomy who received extended perioperative antibiotic therapy. Exposure to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was the only identifiable risk factor for a complication. These findings should be considered when counseling patients on the risks of perioperative antimicrobial therapy at percutaneous nephrolithotomy.

title: [Rational use of medications in the treatment of urinary infections].
authors: León González E, Calderón Ubeda J, Hernández Martín P, Rodríguez Martínez B, Merino Segovia R, Gil García M
abstract: MAIN: to encourage the rational use of medication in the treatment of uncomplicated acute cystitis (UAC). SECONDARY: to find the most common germs in our area and their sensitivity to medication, the most common anti-microbials used and patients age, and to evaluate the savings made through a policy of rational use of medication.Design. Retrospective, descriptive, observational study. La Solana Health Centre jointly with the biochemistry laboratory of the Talavera Area. Probabilistic randomised sampling of clinical histories of women between 20 and 80 with episodes of UAC (349 in all) between 01/10/95 and 01/10/00. First, the laboratory evaluated 591 urine cultures of complicated/uncomplicated UTI from 01/01/00 to 01/10/00, with study of the germs involved and their sensitivities. 373 positives were isolated: E. coli (78.3%), which had the greatest sensitivity to amoxycillin/clavulanic acid, fosfomycin, nitrofurantoin and cefixime; Proteus (7.2%) and Streptococcus D (5.8%). Second, clinical records were analysed for the following: antibiotics (norfloxacine and cyprofloxacine, the most common); length of treatment (average of 6.52.34 days); age of patient (greater number in under-65s). E. coli is the most common germ in UTI and is highly sensitive to amoxy/clavulanic acid, nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin and cefixime. Resistance to cyprofloxacine and norfloxacine are starting to be significant. In UAC the three-day model should be encouraged for young women; and 7 days is recommended for the over-65s. More rational use of medication would increase efficacy and suppose a considerable economic saving in our area.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population includes women with episodes of uncomplicated acute cystitis (relevant UTIs, though not explicitly rUTI). 2) Conducted in a health centre with urine cultures—clinical/real-world setting. 3) The study evaluates treatment/rational antibiotic use for acute cystitis, not prophylactic antibiotic regimens for rUTI. 4) No prophylaxis aimed at preventing recurrent episodes; focus is on acute management and resistance/sensitivity. 5) Reports antibiotic sensitivity/resistance patterns (e.g., E. coli sensitivity and resistance to fluoroquinolones). 6) Retrospective observational descriptive study, not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
reviewer_2_rationale: Both studies involve women with urinary tract infections in clinical/healthcare settings and report antibiotic susceptibility/resistance information, with study designs that are original (not systematic reviews).
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: The provided content is a ScienceDirect access/captcha/403 page rather than the study full text. Without study methods, participant characteristics, intervention details (prophylaxis regimen), outcomes, or resistance data, it is impossible to confirm any PICO criteria or extract resistance results.
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: The provided content contains only a ScienceDirect 403/Captcha blocking page with no study text (methods, participants, interventions, outcomes, or resistance data). Therefore it cannot be verified that the study enrolled women with recurrent UTI, used prophylactic antibiotics, included a comparator, reported antibiotic resistance outcomes, used an eligible human empirical design, or provided extractable resistance results.

title: Antibiotic/adjuvant combinations (ceftriaxone + sulbactam + adjuvant disodium edetate) as an alternative empiric therapy for the treatment of nosocomial infections: Results of a retrospective study.
authors: Chakravorty S, Arun P
abstract: Carbapenems are one of the last therapeutic options to treat various bacterial infections including multidrug resistant (MDR) nosocomial infections. However, excessive and inappropriate prescription of this drug has recently led to an epidemic rise in carbapenem resistance. Optimizing antibiotic utilization and exploring alternate options can be a potential way to control carbapenem resistance. The aim of this study was to assess the clinical efficacy of novel antibiotic adjuvant entity (ceftriaxone + sulbactam + ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid [EDTA] [CSE-1034]) in the treatment of various nosocomial infections. Older patients suffering from hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and complicated urinary tract infections who received CSE-1034 as empirical therapy were evaluated. CSE-1034 therapy was initiated empirically and continued based on the results of culture sensitivity and clinical outcome. In total, 59 culture-positive patients with mean age of 57 ± 19 years were evaluated in this retrospective study. Escherichia coli was the most predominant pathogen isolated, followed by Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumonia, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Microbial sensitivity analysis has shown that isolates from all patients exhibited resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics. Isolated pathogens from 78% were sensitive to meropenem, 86% to CSE-1034, and 100% to colistin except Proteus species. Overall assessment of clinical outcome has shown that 83% cases were cured with CSE-1034 monotherapy, 12% with CSE-1034 and colistin combination therapy, and 5% were cured with alternate meropenem therapy. From this study, it can be concluded that ceftriaxone + sulbactam + EDTA alone or in combination with colistin can be an effective empiric treatment of various MDR nosocomial infections and can serve as an effective alternative to carbapenems.
reviewer_1_rationale: Population includes patients with complicated urinary tract infections in a hospitalized setting. It evaluates an antibiotic-based prophylactic/adjunct regimen aimed at treating urinary tract infections as part of empiric therapy. The abstract reports culture sensitivity/resistance profiles (e.g., susceptibility rates to CSE-1034 vs meropenem/colistin) and clinical cure outcomes. However, it is a retrospective treatment/empiric therapy study in nosocomial MDR infections rather than prophylaxis for rUTIs, and the outcome is treatment efficacy rather than resistance changes from prophylaxis exposure.
reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Human clinical population with complicated urinary tract infections (rUTI-like) and other nosocomial infections. 2) Hospital/nosocomial context. 3) Evaluates an antibiotic regimen (ceftriaxone+sulbactam+EDTA) as empiric therapy. 4) Antibiotic aimed at treating bacterial infection (not diagnostic/other unrelated exposure). 5) Reports microbial sensitivity/resistance (e.g., % sensitive to meropenem vs CSE-1034) though without standard breakpoint details and not specifically isolated to rUTIs only. 6) Explicitly described as a retrospective study (original study), not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population: Although it includes complicated UTI among mixed hospital-acquired infections (HAP/VAP/cUTI), the study is not limited to women with rUTIs; participants are not defined as women with recurrent UTI. 2) Intervention/Exposure: This is empirical treatment of acute nosocomial infections (hospital-acquired pneumonia/VAP/cUTI), with therapy continued/changed based on culture; there is no continuous or postcoital prophylaxis regimen. 3) Comparator: No placebo/no-prophylaxis group and no self-comparison designed to attribute resistance changes to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome: Reports baseline susceptibility proportions to antibiotics for isolated pathogens, but not antibiotic resistance emergence over time or resistance outcomes attributable to prophylaxis exposure (and not rUTI-specific). 5) Study Design: Retrospective human empirical evaluation (observational) with microbiology and clinical outcomes—eligible design type. 6) Data Availability: Resistance data are presented as single timepoint susceptibility rates; insufficient to extract prophylaxis–resistance relationship (no longitudinal resistance outcomes relevant to rUTI prophylaxis).
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Population: Includes hospitalized patients with HAP/VAP and nosocomial complicated UTI; not women with recurrent UTI (rUTI) and no recurrent-Uti criteria. 2) Intervention: Ceftriaxone+sulbactam+EDTA is given as empirical treatment for an acute nosocomial episode; no continuous/postcoital prophylaxis strategy evaluated. 3) Comparator: No placebo/no-prophylaxis comparison and no pre–post within-person resistance assessment attributable to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome: Reports baseline/susceptibility proportions to antibiotics for isolates and clinical cure; does not assess development of resistance over time as a consequence of prophylactic exposure. 5) Design: Retrospective human observational study with culture and susceptibility testing (eligible study type), but not for the prophylaxis/rUTI PICO. 6) Data availability: Resistance results are available descriptively, but not in an extractable way for prophylaxis-resistance causal effects (no relevant prophylaxis comparison and no longitudinal resistance outcomes).

title: Incidence, risk factors and causative bacteria of urinary tract infections and their antimicrobial sensitivity patterns in toddlers and children: A report from two tertiary care hospitals.
authors: Amin EK, Abo Zaid AM, I Kotb AER, El-Gamasy MA
abstract: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is one of the most common bacterial infections among children. It is noted that the risk of renal damage from UTI is the greatest in children younger than five years, thus early diagnosis and prompt treatment are important. The aim of this study was to assess the incidence of UTI in children attending pediatric outpatient clinics in Zagazig and Tanta University Hospitals as tertiary care hospitals. Furthermore, we attempted to determine related risk factors, isolate the organisms that cause UTI in children, and study their antibiotic susceptibility patterns. This cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted on 1200 toddlers and children, (754 boys and 446 girls) aged between 30 months and seven years attending the pediatric outpatient clinics of Zagazig and Tanta University Hospitals. All patient groups were subjected to full medical history, physical examination, dipstick analysis by using both nitrite and leukocyte esterase (LE) detectors, microscopic examinations, and urine culture for cases with the positive LE, positive nitrite dipstick test for urine or positive for both LE and nitrite. The incidence of UTI among children included in the current study was 7%. Positive LE was seen in 112 (9.3%), nitrite positivity was seen in 94 (7.8%), and both LE and nitrite positivity in 34 (2.8%). Escherichia coli was the most common organism. Cefotaxime and amikacin were the most common sensitive antibiotics to the isolates.
reviewer_1_rationale: Population is children/toddlers rather than women with recurrent UTIs. Study is clinical/outpatient (tertiary care hospitals) and includes antibiotic susceptibility outcomes for causative bacteria, but it evaluates incidence/risk factors and treatment susceptibility patterns rather than prophylactic antibiotic exposure. Not a systematic review/meta-analysis; it is an original cross-sectional descriptive study.
reviewer_2_rationale: Population is clearly children/toddlers with urinary tract infections (relevant human clinical context). Conducted in pediatric outpatient clinics in tertiary care hospitals. Exposure/intervention is antibiotic use in relation to susceptibility/resistance patterns (antimicrobial sensitivity outcomes reported). Although not framed as prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis, it is targeted to antimicrobial use for UTI organisms (likely to include/reflect resistance outcome domain). Outcome includes antibiotic susceptibility patterns of isolated causative bacteria (within AMR outcome domain). Study is a cross-sectional descriptive original study, not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: Cross-sectional descriptive study of toddlers/children (30 months–7 years) with UTI incidence and antimicrobial susceptibility; does not enroll women with recurrent UTI (rUTI) specifically, contains no prophylactic antibiotic intervention (no continuous/postcoital prophylaxis, only susceptibility to causative organisms), provides no appropriate comparison for prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis, and does not evaluate resistance emergence/change attributable to prophylaxis. No eligible human empirical design focused on prophylaxis resistance outcomes, and no extractable prophylaxis–resistance relationship.
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: Cross-sectional descriptive study of toddlers/children (not women) assessing incidence and antimicrobial susceptibility of uropathogens; no enrollment of women with recurrent UTI, no prophylactic antibiotic exposure (only diagnostic/treatment context implied), no comparator/no prophylaxis group or longitudinal within-person resistance measurements, and no study design or data structure linking prophylaxis to resistance over time.

title: Pattern of urinary tract infection in Kashmir and antimicrobial susceptibility.
authors: Ahmad S
abstract: Antibiotic resistance of urinary tract pathogens has increased worldwide. The purpose of this study is to provide information regarding the causative agents of urinary tract infection in Kashmiri patients, identify the uropathogens responsible for the infection and study the antibiotic susceptibility patterns of the uropathogens. Clean voided mid-stream urine samples were collected from 2190 patients. The specimens were cultured and the isolates were identified using standard microbiological techniques. The antibiotic susceptibilities of the isolates were also determined. Of 2190 specimens, 591 (27%) showed significant growth upon culture. Approximately 84.1% (497/591) of the 591 patients with UTI were females, most of which belonged to the 21-30 age group (206). The males accounted for 15.9% (94/591) UTI cases. Most of the male patients belonged to the 21-30 age group (34). The lowest incidence of urinary tract infections was seen among the 13-20 years age group. Throughout this study males accounted for only 16% of all UTI cases. Escherichia coli was the most predominant isolate, 53.8% followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae 22.4% and Pseudomonas aeruginosa 7.6%. All isolates were fully sensitive to ofloxacin, and more than 94% were sensitive to cefuroxime. Apart from group D Streptococcus, the overall response to ampicillin by all isolates was less than 15%. The prevalence of multi-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in community-acquired urinary tract infections is increasing. All Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates were fully susceptible to cefuroxime and ofloxacin. It is recommended that cefuroxime and ofloxacin or both are used in the blind treatment of urinary tract infection while awaiting the culture and sensitivity results. Concurrent with the necessary shift in the prescription pattern, attention should be paid to restriction of antibiotic abuse in the community to retard development of further drug resistance.
reviewer_1_rationale: This original clinical microbiology study includes a relevant human population with urinary tract infection (predominantly women) in a real-world clinical/community setting, evaluates antibiotic susceptibility profiles of uropathogens, and reports resistance outcomes (e.g., sensitivities to ofloxacin/cefuroxime and low susceptibility to ampicillin; mention of multidrug resistance in P. aeruginosa). Although it is not specifically a prophylactic regimen for rUTI, the paper is clearly an original study reporting antibiotic resistance/susceptibility outcomes, so it meets inclusion screening criteria through criterion 5; it is not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Population: Studies patients with urinary tract infection and provides sex/age distribution, which plausibly includes women with rUTIs. 2) Setting: Community/real-world outpatient patient sampling (urine from Kashmiri patients), consistent with a clinical human healthcare context. 3) Intervention/exposure: No prophylactic antibiotic use (or any specific prophylaxis regimen) is evaluated; it is a descriptive susceptibility study. 4) Comparator/target: No prophylaxis-directed comparison or target prevention process is assessed—focus is on empirical treatment susceptibility patterns. 5) Outcome: Reports antibiotic susceptibility/resistance profiles of uropathogens (e.g., resistance to ampicillin; susceptibility to cefuroxime/ofloxacin), which is within the AMR outcome domain. 6) Study design: Original cross-sectional/observational microbiology study (not a systematic review/meta-analysis).
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: This paper is a cross-sectional microbiology/antimicrobial susceptibility survey of urine culture isolates from 2190 patients (mostly mixed sexes), not a study of women with recurrent UTI and no prophylactic antibiotic intervention (continuous/postcoital or similar) is evaluated. There is no comparator/placebo/no-prophylaxis arm and no longitudinal pre/post prophylaxis within-person design to attribute resistance change to prophylaxis. Outcomes are descriptive susceptibility to antibiotics, not resistance emergence attributable to prophylaxis. The design is not an empirical prophylaxis study, and resistance results are not linked to any prophylaxis-resistance relationship (no dosing/timing/adherence or effect estimates extractable for the PICO).
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Population: The study enrolls 2190 patients (mostly mixed sex) with UTI symptoms and culture-confirmed growth; it does not specifically define or enroll women with recurrent UTI (rUTI). 2) Intervention/Exposure: No prophylactic antibiotic regimen (continuous/postcoital) is described or evaluated; antibiotics are discussed only in context of empirical treatment/susceptibility. 3) Comparator: No placebo/no-prophylaxis/alternative prophylaxis comparison and no within-person longitudinal pre/post resistance attributable to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome: Reports antimicrobial susceptibility/resistance patterns of uropathogens from urine isolates (e.g., sensitivity of isolates to antibiotics), which is directly resistance-related. 5) Study Design: Cross-sectional laboratory surveillance of isolates from patients; not an eligible human empirical design assessing resistance change due to prophylaxis exposure in women with rUTI. 6) Data Availability: While resistance rates/susceptibility are available, there are no extractable data linking resistance to prophylaxis vs a comparator (no prophylaxis exposure effect estimates for any relevant relationship).

title: Is it possible to extrapolate the rates of resistance of Escherichia coli from asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women to those of E. coli in uncomplicated community-acquired UTI?
authors: Asenjo A, Grados MC, Oteo-Iglesias J, Alós JI
abstract: Treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections in primary care is generally empirical without requesting urine culture and based on biased resistance data collected from selected patients, most of them having risk factors for the isolation of resistant microorganisms. In order to overcome the lack of information on the real resistance rates in uncomplicated UTI, we compared antimicrobial phenotype and genotype of Escherichia coli isolated from pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria (culture always performed) with those from women with uncomplicated acute cystitis (culture rarely performed) of different age groups. Between September 2017 and March 2018, 103 urines were randomly collected from pregnant women aged between 16 and 47 with asymptomatic bacteriuria (AB) (n=42), not hospitalized women in the same age range with uncomplicated acute cystitis (UAC) (n=31) and women older than 47 not hospitalized with UAC (n=30). Bacteria identification was performed using mass spectrometry and the antibiogram by broth microdilution. Genetic typification was carried out by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis. There are no significant differences between the groups of patients in the antibiotic susceptibility. Likewise, as expected, a wide genetic diversity is observed among the strains of E. coli studied without significant differences between the three groups. We propose a simple model that could provide better guidance for selection of empirical antimicrobial therapy for non-pregnant women with UAC than do generic hospital antibiogram data based on reliably extrapolating the susceptibility data of strains isolated from pregnant women with AB as representation of women with community-acquired UAC.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Human study involves women with asymptomatic bacteriuria and uncomplicated acute cystitis (relevant to rUTI-related epidemiology). 2) Conducted in outpatient/non-hospital settings with urine collection/culture. 3) Exposure relates to antimicrobial susceptibility/antibiogram comparisons of E. coli across groups (antibiotic resistance assessment). 4) Not a direct prophylaxis regimen, but it targets the antibiotic-resistance outcome in UTI-related pathogens (plausibly within review’s resistance outcomes domain). 5) Reports antibiotic susceptibility (phenotype/antibiogram) and genetic diversity, i.e., resistance outcomes. 6) Appears to be an original cross-sectional/comparative study with laboratory testing, not a systematic review.
reviewer_2_rationale: Population is pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria and non-hospitalized women with uncomplicated cystitis; this is related to community UTI but not the target population of women with rUTIs. Setting is not clearly a real intervention/prophylaxis clinical trial; it appears to be a comparative resistance characterization study, so the intervention context (rUTI/prophylaxis) is not met. No prophylactic antibiotic exposure/intervention is evaluated; it compares resistance phenotypes/genotypes across patient groups. Comparator is not relevant (no prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis). Outcomes are antibiotic susceptibility/resistance rates but they are not reported in relation to prophylaxis effects nor rUTI prophylactic use. Not a systematic review/meta-analysis; it is an original laboratory/observational resistance comparison study.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population: NO — includes pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria and women with uncomplicated acute cystitis, but not a study population of women with recurrent UTI (rUTI) specifically. 2) Intervention/Exposure: NO — there is no prophylactic antibiotic intervention (continuous/postcoital/none) studied; it is a microbiology susceptibility/genotype comparison. 3) Comparator: NO — there is a comparison between AB vs UAC strain susceptibility, but this does not assess the effect of prophylaxis vs no prophylaxis to attribute resistance change to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome: YES — reports antibiotic susceptibility/resistance phenotypes by organism (percentage susceptible across multiple agents), directly derived from urine culture antibiograms (e.g., ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, cotrimoxazole). 5) Study Design: NO — despite being human empirical microbiology work, it is not an eligible design for prophylaxis-resistance (no RCT/cohort of prophylaxis; no recurrence/prophylaxis exposure). 6) Data Availability: NO — resistance data are extractable for susceptibility patterns, but there is no prophylaxis-resistance relationship or extractable effect estimate for prophylaxis (since no prophylaxis regimen/exposure exists).
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: Population includes pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria and non-hospitalized women with uncomplicated acute cystitis, but not a cohort/trial of women with recurrent UTI (rUTI) as the study’s enrollment target. Prophylactic antibiotics are not administered; exposure is not prophylaxis but naturally occurring isolates from different clinical states. There is no prophylaxis vs no-prophylaxis comparator (and no pre/post within-person resistance attribution to prophylaxis). Resistance/susceptibility phenotypes are reported via broth microdilution antibiograms (table 1/2) for multiple antibiotics. Study design is a cross-sectional comparative sampling of isolates (and includes external 2017 laboratory cumulative data), not an eligible human empirical design assessing prophylactic antibiotic effects on resistance development. Resistance data are extractable, but they are not linked to any prophylaxis intervention or randomized/longitudinal resistance change attributable to prophylaxis.

title: [Clinical features and antibiotic resistance of Escherichia coli bloodstream infections in children].
authors: Li S, Guo L, Liu L, Dong F, Liu G
abstract: To analyze risk factors, clinical features, outcomes and antibiotic resistance of Escherichia coli(E.coli) causing bloodstream infections in children. All inpatients with E. coli positive blood culture in Beijing Children's Hospital from January 2012 to May 2014 were enrolled; 112 cases were included, 66 cases (58.9%) were male, and 46 cases(41.1%) were female. Age range was 2 days to 16 years. Among them, 43 cases (38.4%) were neonates, 19 cases (17.0%) aged from 1 month to 1 year, 14 cases (12.5%) were 1-3 years old, and 36 cases (32.1%) were over three years old. We analyzed the divisions to which the patients were admitted, source of infection, underlying diseases, clinical characteristics, antibiotic resistance, and treatment outcomes, etc. Forty-six cases (41.1%) were treated in division of hematology, 42 (37.5%) in neonatology, 9 (8.0%) in internal medicine, 8 (7.1%) in surgery, and 7 (6.3%) in pediatric intensive care unit. Sixty-five cases(58.0%) had underlying diseases. Fever was the most frequently presented symptom, as it was seen in 91 cases (81.3%); 52 cases(46.4%) had respiratory symptoms. Among these, 43 cases had pneumonia, 3 cases had respiratory failure, 3 cases were diagnosed as upper respiratory tract infection, 2 had pulmonary hemorrhage and 1 case had bronchitis. Twenty-six cases (23.2%)were diagnosed as severe sepsis and purulent meningitis separately, 14 cases(12.5%) had urinary tract infection. There were 73 (65.2%) strains inducing extended spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs), of which 6 (8.2%) and 10 (13.7%) strains were resistant to amikacin and carbapenems respectively. Resistance rate against other antimicrobial agents varied from 64.6% to 100%. 92 (82.1%) cases were cured or had improvement while 20 patients (17.9%) died or could not be cured at the end of treatment. Positive ESBLs (χ(2) = 6.609, P = 0.010), being complicated with severe sepsis (χ(2) = 40.253, P = 0.000) and requiring mechanical ventilation (χ(2) = 34.441, P = 0.000) indicate poor prognosis. Patients with underlying diseases and newborns are susceptible to E. coli bloodstream infection. ESBLs infection, severe sepsis and mechanical ventilation indicate poor prognosis in E. coli blood stream infection. Clinicians may use carbapenems as empirical treatment for ESBLs infection. There may be carbapenem-resistant enterobacteriaceae strains infection if patients receiving treatment with carbapenems have no response.
reviewer_1_rationale: Paper 40176149 is a systematic review/meta-analysis (explicitly), so excluded by design, despite AMR reporting. Paper 26875468 is an original clinical study of children with E. coli bloodstream infections (not the target rUTI female prophylaxis setting), but it includes antibiotic resistance outcomes; population/setting and intervention (prophylactic antibiotics for rUTIs in women) are not met, so it should not be included for this RUTI prophylaxis/AMR linkage review.
reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Pediatric inpatients with E. coli positive blood cultures (bloodstream infections) are clearly a relevant human population with infectious disease context. 2) Hospital-based recruitment (Beijing Children’s Hospital inpatient divisions) is a real clinical setting. 3) The study evaluates antibiotic exposure/treatment context insofar as it characterizes antibiotic resistance patterns among isolates. 4) Resistance pertains to E. coli bloodstream infection management (not a diagnostic-only or unrelated intervention). 5) Outcome includes antibiotic resistance (e.g., ESBL prevalence and resistance rates to multiple antimicrobial agents). 6) Appears to be an original observational cohort/retrospective study of cases (not a systematic review/meta-analysis), though it does not clearly assess prophylactic antibiotic use specifically.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population: NO — enrolls children with E. coli bloodstream infection; not women with recurrent UTI. 2) Intervention/Exposure: NO — no prophylactic antibiotic regimen (continuous/postcoital) assessed; this is infection/bacteremia characterization. 3) Comparator: NO — no prophylaxis vs placebo/no prophylaxis or resistance-relevant longitudinal comparison. 4) Outcome: NO — reports general antimicrobial resistance in blood isolates, not rUTI prophylaxis-related resistance emergence/susceptibility in urine with defined prophylaxis exposure. 5) Study Design: YES — human empirical clinical study (112 pediatric cases; observational analysis). 6) Data Availability: NO — resistance data are extractable for bloodstream isolates, but not linked to any prophylaxis-resistance relationship (no prophylaxis exposure/time course).
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: 本研究为儿童（含新生儿）大肠埃希菌血流感染的回顾性/观察性分析，未招募“女性rUTI（复发性尿路感染）”人群；不存在预防性抗生素暴露（连续/经性交后等）与对照组/安慰剂比较；虽报告了细菌对多种抗菌药物的耐药率（如ESBLs相关、阿米卡星/碳青霉烯耐药率），但研究对象为血培养分离株而非rUTI尿培养中的前后耐药发展，且研究设计与结局框架不支持“预防用药导致rUTI相关耐药”的因果评估；同时不提供可用于抽取“预防性抗生素 vs 无预防”耐药效应估计的数据。

title: Individual health insurance data of antibiotic delivery in previous months as a tool to predict bacterial resistance of urinary tract infection: A prospective cohort study.
authors: Alexandre K, Gillibert A, Dahyot S, Fabre R, Kuhn F, Benichou J, Delbos V, Caron F
abstract: We aimed to quantify the individual risk of antimicrobial resistance among patients with community-acquired Escherichia coli urinary tract infection (UTI) according to their antibiotic exposure over the previous 18 months. French patients were prospectively recruited in two centers in 2015-2017. Resistance of isolates to amoxicillin (AMX), amoxicillin-clavulanate (AMC), third-generation cephalosporins (3GC), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), fluoroquinolones (FQ) and fosfomycin (FOS) was analysed according to previous intra-class and inter-class antibiotic exposure documented in health insurance files. Previous antibiotic exposure was found in 588 (81.4 %) of the 722 UTI cases analysed (564 patients). Recent exposure (three months before UTI) was associated with stronger intra-class impact on E. coli resistance compared to remote exposure (18 months before UTI) for AMX, AMC, FQ and TMP-SMX, with respective adjusted odds ratios [95 % confidence interval] of 1.63 [1.20-2.21], 1.59 [1.02-2.48], 3.01 [1.90-4.77], and 2.60 [1.75-3.87]. AMX, FQ, and TMP-SMX also showed significant inter-class impact. Resistance to 3GC was not significantly associated with intraclass exposure (adjusted OR: 0.88 [0.41-1.90]). FOS resistance was remarkably low (0.4 %). Duration of the antibiotic-free period required for resistance risk to drop below 10 %, the threshold for empirical use in UTI, was modelled as < 1 month for 3GC, >18 months for AMX and TMP-SMX and uncertain for AMC (5.2 months [2.3 to > 18]) and FQ (17.4 months [7.4 to > 18]). Resistance of E. coli causing UTI is partially predicted by previous personal antibiotic delivery.
reviewer_1_rationale: Prospective cohort in French patients with community-acquired E. coli UTI assessing prior antibiotic exposure from health insurance data (antibiotic delivery) as the exposure/prophylaxis-like risk factor. Reports clinically relevant antibiotic resistance outcomes (susceptibility/resistance to multiple antibiotic classes) and quantifies associations via adjusted odds ratios; not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
reviewer_2_rationale: Prospective cohort of French patients with community-acquired E. coli UTI evaluating prior antibiotic exposure (from health insurance records) over preceding 18 months. Resistance outcomes for multiple antibiotic classes are analyzed (e.g., AMX, AMC, 3GC, TMP-SMX, FQ, FOS) and reported as adjusted odds ratios, implying defined resistance testing/breakpoints though not fully detailed in the abstract. Setting is real-world healthcare/insurance data linked to clinical UTI episodes, and design is original (not a review).
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: Unable to access the paper full text due to ScienceDirect 403/captcha interstitial. No information available on population (women with rUTI), prophylactic regimen, comparator, resistance outcomes, study design, or extractable resistance data; therefore all criteria cannot be verified.
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: Unable to access the paper’s full text (ScienceDirect 403/captcha). No information is available to confirm: (1) enrollment of women with recurrent UTI, (2) prophylactic antibiotic exposure, (3) presence of an appropriate comparator, (4) reporting of antibiotic resistance from urine culture results, (5) eligible human empirical study design, or (6) extractable resistance outcomes/effect estimates.

title: Causative organism of urinary tract infection and drug resistance in children at child's Central Teaching Hospital in Baghdad City.
authors: Abdul Raheem RS, Hussein MA, Al-Din NI
abstract: To identify antibiotic susceptibility and resistance of bacterial strains responsible for urinary tract infections in children. The cross-sectional study was conducted from June to December 2017 at the Central Teaching Hospital, Baghdad, Iraq, and comprised patients aged between one day and 15 years who were brought to the emergency department and were diagnosed as having urinary tract infections. Urine samples were cultured on appropriate media and the isolated organisms were identified. The susceptibility of bacteria-causing urinary tract infection to different antimicrobial agents was investigated using antibiotic discs. Data was analysed using SPSS 24. Of the 155 patients, 78(50.3%) were girls and 77(49.7%) were boys. The highest number of patients 55(35.5%) were aged <1 year. The most common organism encountered in the study were Escherichia coli 78(50.followed by Klebsiella pneumonia 21(13.5%). Among the Escherichia coli isolates,54(69.2%) were resistant to ceftriaxone, 50(64.1%)to ampicillin and 38(48.7%) to ciprofloxacin. Escherichia coli was found to be most predominant organism causing urinary tract infection, and it was resistant, among others, to ceftriaxone, ampicillin and ciprofloxacin.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population includes children with diagnosed urinary tract infections; rUTI prophylaxis population is not specified. 2) Hospital-based clinical context (emergency department) with real-world specimen culture. 3) No prophylactic antibiotic regimen is evaluated—only antibiotic susceptibility/resistance in acute pediatric UTI pathogens. 4) The antibiotic assessment is directed at treatment susceptibility for current infection, not prophylaxis for recurrent UTIs in women. 5) Resistance outcomes are clearly reported (e.g., E. coli resistance to ceftriaxone/ampicillin/ciprofloxacin). 6) Cross-sectional original study; not a systematic review/meta-analysis.
reviewer_2_rationale: Prospective cohort of community-acquired E. coli UTI in French women/UTI cases; exposure is prior antibiotic delivery (prophylaxis-like antibiotic use over 18 months); compares stronger resistance associations with recent vs remote exposure; reports antibiotic resistance outcomes (e.g., adjusted ORs to multiple drug classes with CIs and modeled time to risk drop); original study design (cohort), not a review.

title: Prediction of infection caused by extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae: development of a clinical decision-making nomogram.
authors: García-Tello A, Gimbernat H, Redondo C, Meilán E, Arana DM, Cacho J, Dorado JF, Angulo JC
abstract: This study aimed to assess the population at risk of infection by extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing organisms, using clinical criteria. All urine cultures positive for Enterobacteriaceae in a Spanish hospital department from January 2010 to 2014 were reviewed. All isolates with ESBL-positive strains were collected, and isolates received during the first week of each month with ESBL-negative strains from symptomatic patients hospitalized or admitted to the emergency room. Multivariate analysis of the factors involved was undertaken and a nomogram developed to predict the probability of infection by ESBL-producing microorganisms. The study included 1524 patients with urinary tract infection (UTI): 416 ESBL-positive and 1108 ESBL-negative. In univariate analysis, risk factors were: male gender (p = 0.036), age (p < 0.0001), nursing home (p < 0.0001), previous antimicrobial therapy (p < 0.0001) or hospitalization (p < 0.0001), diabetes (p < 0.0001), chronic renal insufficiency (p < 0.0001), severe underlying disease (p < 0.0001), neoplasia (p = 0.0005), urological (p < 0.0001) and non-urological invasive procedure (p = 0.0003), recurrent UTI (p < 0.0001), urological (p < 0.0001) or abdominal surgery (p < 0.0001) and permanent urethral catheter (p < 0.0001). In multivariate analysis, the data set was split into a development cohort of 1067 patients and a validation cohort of 457 cases. A nomogram was developed to predict the probability of infection by ESBL-producing bacteria, which included seven variables: age (p < 0.0001), gender (p = 0.004), nursing home (p < 0.0001), previous antimicrobial therapy (p = 0.04) or hospitalization (p < 0.0001), recurrent UTI (p < 0.0001) and non-urological invasive procedure (p = 0.005). The discriminative accuracy was 0.79 (95% confidence interval 0.77-0.83). A nomogram was developed that predicts the risk of infection by ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae with reasonable accuracy. It could improve clinical decision making and enable more efficient empirical treatment.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population includes patients with UTI (including those with recurrent UTI) but not limited to women with rUTIs. 2) Conducted in a hospital/ED setting with reviewed urine cultures. 3) Study exposure is clinical risk prediction for ESBL organisms, not prophylactic antibiotic use. 4) The target is diagnosing/predicting ESBL infection risk, not evaluating a prophylactic antibiotic regimen for rUTI. 5) Outcome includes clinically relevant microbiologic resistance phenotype (ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae) and includes recurrent UTI as a predictor, so the resistance outcome domain is covered. 6) Original retrospective observational cohort/derivation-validation study (not a systematic review).
reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Participants are patients with urinary tract infection/Enterobacteriaceae urine cultures, relevant to women with rUTIs (population is UTI patients; sex not guaranteed in abstract). 2) Conducted in a Spanish hospital department with hospitalized/ED patients—clinical setting. 3) Exposure/intervention is prior antimicrobial therapy and hospitalization as risk factors; this is a relevant pharmacologic exposure category for AMR outcomes. 4) The study targets risk of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae in UTIs (directly related to antibiotic resistance in the infection context, not an unrelated mechanism). 5) Outcome is probability/risk of ESBL-producing organisms (antibiotic resistance) based on urine culture results; includes quantitative modeling outputs (e.g., cohort sizes and predictive performance). 6) Appears to be an original observational development/validation study (not described as a systematic review/meta-analysis).
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population: includes 1524 UTI patients of unspecified sex mix; not women-with-rUTI enrolled as a study population (only “recurrent UTI” as a risk factor). 2) Intervention/Exposure: no prophylactic antibiotic regimen (it’s a prediction/nomogram study based on urine culture and clinical factors). 3) Comparator: no placebo/no-prophylaxis design and no within-person pre/post prophylaxis framework. 4) Outcome: focuses on ESBL status (predicting ESBL-producing infection), not antibiotic resistance emergence or susceptibility changes attributable to prophylaxis; no prophylaxis-resistance relationship. 5) Design: eligible human empirical observational study (retrospective urine culture review/development-validation cohorts). 6) Data availability: resistance data are not presented as a prophylaxis-driven resistance outcome (and no extractable estimates of prophylaxis-related resistance change).
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: 1) Population includes all UTI patients from hospital cultures; women with rUTI are not the enrolled population/target subset (rUTI is only a risk factor variable). 2) No prophylactic antibiotic exposure is administered/evaluated; “previous antimicrobial therapy” is observational history. 3) No comparison group for prophylaxis vs none/placebo/alternative, nor a within-person resistance change attributable to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome is prediction of ESBL infection probability (case-control style), not antibiotic resistance/susceptibility patterns or resistance development due to prophylaxis. 5) Human empirical observational study using urine cultures and multivariable modeling—eligible design type. 6) From the provided content, resistance outcomes extractable for prophylaxis-resistance relationships are not available (focus is ESBL status and modeling, not longitudinal susceptibility effect estimates).

title: Emerging antibiotic resistance among the uropathogens.
authors: Ram S, Gupta R, Gaheer M
abstract: A total of 18,876 urine samples from patients of clinically suspected UTI including asymptomatic pregnant females were analysed, during the year 1997 & 1998. Culture positivity rate was found to be 37%. The incidence of Proteus was on the rise during the year 1998 especially in hospitalized patients. The antibiotic sensitivity pattern of uropathogens was also analysed to check the emergence of drug resistance. This study has revealed that withdrawal of a particular antibiotic due to high level of resistance observed during previous years, has led to re-emergence of antibiotic sensitive mutants. Further indiscriminate use of newer antibiotics like amikacin and netilimicin is responsible for emergeny of resistant variant against these antibiotics and this lays stress upon the immediate need for national antibiotic policy.
reviewer_1_rationale: Includes asymptomatic pregnant females and clinically suspected UTIs with urine culture and antibiotic susceptibility/resistance patterns of uropathogens, in a clinical setting. However, there is no evaluation of a prophylactic antibiotic regimen for women with recurrent UTIs; it is an observational surveillance/analysis of resistance trends and effects of prior antibiotic withdrawal/use rather than rUTI prophylaxis exposure.
reviewer_2_rationale: Abstract involves human patients with suspected UTI (including pregnant females) with urine culture and reports antibiotic sensitivity/resistance patterns of uropathogens over time. Mentions withdrawal of a particular antibiotic due to prior high resistance and subsequent re-emergence, implying an antibiotic exposure/policy change related to prophylactic/antibiotic use context, though not specifically rUTI prophylaxis in women. Outcomes are antibiotic resistance (sensitivity patterns) and the study is an original surveillance/observational analysis rather than a review.

title: [Frequency of Haemophilus spp. in urinary and and genital tract samples].
authors: Leskovar V, Mlinarić-Dzepina A, Marijan T, Vranes J
abstract: To determine the prevalence and antibiotic susceptibility of Haemophilus influenzae and H. parainfluenzae isolated from the urinary and genital tracts. Identification of strains bacteria Haemophilus spp. was carried out by using API NH identification system, and antibiotic susceptibility was performed by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method. A total number of 50 (0.03%) H. influenzae and 14 (0.01%) H. parainfluenzae (out of 180, 415 samples) were isolated from genitourinary tract. From urine samples of the girls under 15 years of age these bacteria were isolated in 13 (0.88%) and two (0.13%) cases, respectively, and only in one case (0.11%) of the UTI in boys (H. influenzae). In persons of fertile age, it was only H. influenzae bacteria that was found in urine samples of the five women (0.04%) and in three men (0.22%). As a cause of vulvovaginitis, H. influenzae was isolated in four (5.63%), and H. parainfluenzae in two (2.82%) girls. In persons of fertile age, H. influenzae was isolated from 10 (0.49%) smears of the cervix, and in nine (1.74%) male samples. H. parainfluenzae was isolated from seven (1.36%) male samples. (p < 0.01). Susceptibility testing ofH. influenzae and H. parainfluenzae revealed that both pathogens were significantly resistant to cotrimoxasol only (26.0% and 42.9%, respectively). In the etiology of genitourinary infections of girls during childhood, genital infections of women in fertile age (especially in pregnant women), and men with cases of epididimytis and/or orchitis, it is important to think about this rare and demanding bacteria in terms of cultivation.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Includes genitourinary samples with UTIs/vulvovaginitis and isolated pathogens, but population is not specifically women with recurrent UTI; still involves urinary tract infection context. 2) Conducted on clinical microbiology specimens from patients (girls, women, men), i.e., real-world healthcare setting. 3) No prophylactic antibiotic regimen is evaluated—only prevalence and antibiotic susceptibility testing. 4) Antibiotics are discussed only as susceptibility/resistance profiles, not as prophylaxis directed at rUTI prevention. 5) Reports resistance/susceptibility outcomes (e.g., resistance to cotrimoxazole). 6) Original observational lab/epidemiologic study (not a review).
reviewer_2_rationale: (1) Human participants with genitourinary infections/samples including UTIs are studied. (2) Setting appears clinical/diagnostic microbiology of genital/urinary tract specimens. (3) Exposure/intervention is antibiotic susceptibility measurement (relevant to resistance assessment). (4) Focus is on antibiotic susceptibility of organisms associated with genitourinary infections. (5) Reports resistance/susceptibility findings (e.g., % resistant to cotrimoxazole) though not clearly linked to prophylactic antibiotic use. (6) Appears to be an original prevalence/susceptibility microbiology study, not a review.

title: Drug resistance, serotypes, and phylogenetic groups among uropathogenic Escherichia coli including O25-ST131 in Mexico City.
authors: Molina-López J, Aparicio-Ozores G, Ribas-Aparicio RM, Gavilanes-Parra S, Chávez-Berrocal ME, Hernández-Castro R, Manjarrez-Hernández HÁ
abstract: The increasing prevalence of uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) strains resistant to multiple antibiotics complicates the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs). This study aimed to analyze the antimicrobial resistance, serotypes, and phylogenetic groups among strains of E. coli isolated from outpatients with UTIs in Mexico City. A total of 119 E. coli isolates were recovered from urine samples from outpatients with clinical diagnosis of uncomplicated UTIs from 2004 to 2007. The serotype was assessed by agglutination in microtiter plates; susceptibility to antimicrobials was determined by the disk diffusion method. Clone O25-ST131 and phylogenetic groups of E. coli strains were tested by methods based on PCR multiplex. The predominant serotype was O25:H4 (21.2%). Resistance to antibiotics was ampicillin (83.7%); piperacillin (53.8%); the fluoroquinolone group (55.5-60.6%), and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) (56.4%). Additionally, 36 (30.2%) isolates were multidrug-resistant and 13 of these 36 strains were identified as E. coli O25-ST131 clone by an allele-specific PCR-based assay. Phylogenetic analysis showed that 15 of 17 isolates with serotype O25:H4 belonged to group B2. This is the first report that establishes the presence in Mexico of the O25-ST131 clonal group of E. coli, which has been associated with multidrug-resistance and with high virulence potential. The spread of this clone in Mexico should be monitored closely. We found a correlation between serotype O25:H4 and multidrug resistance in UPEC strains. Our results indicate that the use of ampicillin, fluoroquinolones, and TMP/SMX should be reviewed when selecting empirical therapy for UTIs.
reviewer_1_rationale: This study analyzes antimicrobial resistance and phylogenetic characteristics of E. coli isolates from outpatients with uncomplicated UTIs; it does not describe prophylactic antibiotic use for women with recurrent UTIs, nor report resistance outcomes in the context of prophylaxis exposure. It is an original microbiology/epidemiologic study, not a review.
reviewer_2_rationale: Original molecular epidemiology study of uropathogenic E. coli from outpatient uncomplicated UTI cases (Mexico City), assessing antibiotic susceptibility (disk diffusion) and multidrug resistance among isolates, including O25-ST131. However, it evaluates resistance in relation to clonal/serotype groups rather than prophylactic antibiotic use/exposure, and the abstract does not describe a prophylaxis intervention or comparator; therefore it does not match the intervention PICO, though it is within the resistance outcome domain.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Population: Includes adult outpatients (82 women, 37 men) with uncomplicated UTI; not restricted to women with rUTI by the study definition—no rUTI criteria described. 2) Intervention/exposure: No prophylactic antibiotic regimen; this is baseline antimicrobial susceptibility/epidemiology of isolates from UTIs, not continuous or postcoital prophylaxis. 3) Comparator: No placebo/no-prophylaxis group and no pre–post within-person design to attribute resistance changes to prophylaxis. 4) Outcome: Reports antibiotic resistance prevalence for multiple drugs from cultured isolates, and MDR definitions, plus O25-ST131 identification and phylogenetic associations. 5) Design: Human observational microbiology study using isolates and susceptibility testing. 6) Data availability: Although resistance rates are extractable, there is no prophylaxis-resistance relationship with regimen/dosing/adherence to compute extractable effect estimates for antibiotic prophylaxis.
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: This study is a single timepoint (2004–2007) microbiologic surveillance of E. coli isolates from outpatients with uncomplicated UTIs, not a cohort/trial of women with recurrent UTIs. It does not involve prophylactic antibiotic exposure (continuous/postcoital) versus non-use/placebo/alternative, nor any within-person longitudinal pre/post design to attribute resistance changes to prophylaxis. Outcomes are antibiotic resistance among isolates, but the paper does not analyze resistance development over time or in relation to prophylaxis exposure (no resistance outcome as a function of prophylactic use). Design is cross-sectional observational lab characterization without an empirical intervention/exposure framework required by the PICO, and resistance effect estimates for prophylaxis-resistance relationships are not available.

title: [Five years follow-up of infections with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing enterobacteriaceae].
authors: Fouquet M, Morange V, Bruyère F
abstract: Actually, epidemiology of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) producing enterobacteriaceae is increasing worldwide, especially in urinary tract infections (UTI). The objective of the study was to investigate the epidemiology of ESBL producers in a department of urology. This was a retrospective, monocentric study, which included all patients with positive culture showing an ESBL producing enterobacteriaceae in a department of urology between 2005 and 2009 included. The prevalence of ESBL producers in UTI was 2/113 (1.8%) in 2005 and 3/196 (1.5%) in 2009 (P=0.87). Twenty-seven isolates were included: 66.7% of Escherichia coli, 11.1% of Klebsiella pneumoniae, 11.1% of Enterobacter cloacae. ESBL producers were resistant to another antibiotic family in 24 cases (88.8%). The mean age in this study was 70.4 years, 70% of patients had another antibiotherapy in the past 6 months, 87% an hospitalization within 90% had surgery. Among the patients, 56.5% had a material. The infection was community-acquired in three cases only. Thirty-five percent of patients had no symptoms, 26% presented with severe sepsis. This report was a five-year retrospective study of BLSE-positive bacteria showing the nosocomial infection with ESBL producers and their multiresistance to usual antibiotics without any increase of their prevalence.
reviewer_1_rationale: 1) Target population plausibly includes UTI patients with recurrent/complicated infection contexts. 2) Conducted in a urology department (clinical setting). 3) No prophylactic antibiotic regimen/exposure is evaluated—study is retrospective epidemiology of ESBL-producing infections. 4) Not an intervention directed at preventing rUTIs; focuses on ESBL prevalence and resistance patterns. 5) Reports antibiotic resistance (multiresistance to other antibiotic families) among ESBL producers. 6) Original retrospective observational study (not a review).
reviewer_2_rationale: Population includes patients with urinary tract infections and other urologic infections due to ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, assessed in a urology department (clinical setting). Study evaluates antibiotic resistance characteristics (reported high rates of multiresistance/ESBL prevalence). It is not explicitly a prophylaxis study, but it plausibly relates to antibiotic exposure/management and resistance outcomes. Design is a retrospective original cohort (not a systematic review/meta-analysis). Quantitative prevalence/resistance data are provided, though prophylaxis-specific attribution is not clear in the abstract.
fulltext_reviewer_1_rationale: Access to the actual paper content is blocked (ScienceDirect captcha/403), so there is no information to determine population (women with rUTI), whether prophylactic antibiotic regimens were used, any comparator, whether antibiotic resistance outcomes were reported, study design, or extractable resistance data.
fulltext_reviewer_2_rationale: Full text is not accessible (ScienceDirect captcha/403), so eligibility (rUTI population), prophylaxis intervention, comparator, and antibiotic resistance outcomes cannot be verified or extracted.

title: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation for Recurrent Clostridium difficile Infection Reduces Recurrent Urinary Tract Infection Frequency.
authors: Tariq R, Pardi DS, Tosh PK, Walker RC, Razonable RR, Khanna S
abstract: Broad-spectrum antibiotics for recurrent multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections (UTIs) disrupt the gut microbiome and promote antibiotic resistance. Fecal microbiota transplantation led to resolution of recurrent Clostridium difficile, significantly decreased recurrent UTI frequency, and improved antibiotic susceptibility profile of UTI-causing organisms.
reviewer_1_rationale: The paper involves recurrent UTI frequency outcomes in a human population, but the intervention described is fecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent C. difficile infection rather than prophylactic antibiotic use for rUTIs. It targets C. difficile resolution, not an antibiotic prophylaxis strategy directed at rUTI prevention. While it reports changes in UTI frequency and an improved antibiotic susceptibility profile (relevant to resistance outcomes), the exposure/intervention and comparison do not match the prophylactic antibiotic PICO.
